title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
description:
Justin Reock (Deputy CTO, DX) shares five trends from DX's data on about 200,000 engineers. Deployment frequency is rising, but change failure rate has become far more volatile. Maintainability is up while change confidence is down. PRs have grown from about 44 to 72 lines. Juniors use AI the most, but staff+ engineers save as much time while using fewer tokens. Median gains in PR throughput are around 7.7%, and even top performers didn't reach 2x, because code generation was never the bottleneck. Justin walks through the DX AI Measurement Framework (utilization, impact, cost), how to assess your platform's AI readiness, and "agent experience," which uses feedback from the agents themselves. He closes with case studies of AI applied across the whole SDLC: Morgan Stanley (300K hours saved a year), Zapier (15% more value per engineer, and hiring more) and Spotify (an SRE incident agent).

title: The Chief AI Officer: Scientist, Architect, Coach — Rania Khalaf, WSO2
description:
The Chief AI Officer is one of the fastest-growing roles in tech, and one of the least defined. AI is in everything, so the job can easily turn into everything.

Rania Khalaf (Chief AI Officer, WSO2; previously 20 years at IBM Research, where she ran about a third of the global AI research organization) shares a framework from two years in the role. It splits the job into three focus areas, Scientist, Architect and Coach, each a slider whose setting depends on your company type, its AI maturity and your own skills. She draws on her time at an ag-biotech unicorn, where simple blob detection beat machine learning, and at WSO2, where AI reshaped the product strategy around the agentic enterprise. She explains why she refuses to measure tokens and what she tracks instead: AI fluency across the workforce, depth of adoption, GEO visibility, agent-consumable products (MCP servers, skills, CLIs), agent-proof pricing, earned thought leadership and AI ARR. She closes on why the role needs strong CEO backing, and why sometimes the CPO, or even the head of HR, ends up running AI.

title: The Death of the Code Review: What the Data Actually Says — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
description:
Developers using autonomous agents wrote 741% more code but shipped only 30% more software. The bottleneck is human review, and "just review harder" doesn't scale. Reviewer effectiveness collapses past about 400 lines, and agents now open 10,000-line PRs.

Laurie Voss (Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, co-founder of npm) reviews what the industry is actually doing about it. The evidence covers OpenAI's zero-human-code product, METR's finding that about half of SWE-bench-passing PRs wouldn't be merged, and Cognition's FrontierCode (88% on SWE-bench Pro vs. 29% on real mergeability). She explains why a mergeability benchmark would immediately become a training signal for frontier models. She also covers how Cursor and GitHub run review in production, why multi-pass review and default suspicion cut false positives, and what Carlini's agent-built C compiler and Bun's million-line Zig-to-Rust port (13,044 unsafe blocks) reveal about taking humans out of the loop. Automated reviewers can be fooled by prompt injection that humans catch, which leaves production as the last reviewer standing.

title: Your Agents Are in Solitary Confinement: Why MCP & A2A Aren't Enough — Vlad Luzin, Band
description:
If you run Claude and Codex side by side, one planning and one reviewing, you're doing the job of a network router, passing messages between two stateful agents by hand. Loop engineering hands that job to a script. Neither one lets agents actually work together.

Vlad Luzin (Co-founder & CTO, Band) explains why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem. Bigger context windows don't fix the single-agent bottleneck. Messaging platforms like Slack, Discord and WhatsApp are built for humans and block bot-to-bot traffic. Protocols like MCP and A2A are too low-level: stateless calls, one-way client/server, no discovery, and queues and timeouts you still have to build yourself. He then walks through what's needed: real-time ordered transport, persistence and rehydration, runtime binding across frameworks, agent-first abstractions (participants, rooms, routing) and enterprise governance. Two live demos show Codex, LangGraph, Claude Code and a personal assistant finding each other and collaborating in real time, with full human-in-the-loop visibility.

Join the AI Evals October 2026 cohort: https://maven.com/parlance-labs/evals?promoCode=yt-2026

If you're new to my channel, my name is Hamel Husain. I spent 20 years in data and machine learning at banks, startups, Airbnb, GitHub, before most people knew what any of that meant. In 2023 I started advising AI companies and noticed the same gap everywhere: nobody had a real way to test, measure, and improve their AI products. They were shipping on vibes.

So I started documenting how to fix that. What I built became the most popular evals course in the world: 4,500+ engineers and PMs from OpenAI, Google, Meta, Anthropic, and more. My colleague Shreya Shankar and I are also co-authoring the O'Reilly book on it.

This channel is where I share what I actually know about building AI products that hold up.

How I got here...
2003: Built credit-risk models right out of college (Math and Industrial Engineering). SQL, scripting, data visualization. The foundational stuff.
2005: Data consulting across a dozen industries. Reading messy data and finding where processes were broken. Same muscle I use now for error analysis on LLM products.
2008: Burned out and went to law school. Learned two things: I can write, and I'm an engineer who was kidding himself.
2010: Back to consulting. Predictive models across demand forecasting, marketing, and customer service.
2014: Joined DataRobot to sit near Kaggle grandmasters. Thousands of reps building predictive models fast.
2016: Data Scientist at Airbnb. Inherited a badly overfit growth model that had been running in prod. Helped set up systems so it couldn't happen again.
2017: Machine learning at GitHub. Led the team that built CodeSearchNet, a benchmark for semantic code search. Underneath, it was a set of evals for code understanding. OpenAI later used it to evaluate their first code embeddings, which became groundwork for the earliest coding models.
2022: Left to turn an open source developer tool into a company. ChatGPT shipped and the bet stopped making sense. I walked away.
2023: Independent consultant. Advised 50+ companies, startups to Fortune 500s. Everyone had the same gap: no real way to test or improve AI beyond vibe checks. I started documenting the fix.

This channel is the unfiltered version of what I've learned. What works, what doesn't, and how to build AI that actually holds up.

Hamel

title: 8 Claude Code skills I use for building better AI evals
description:

Shipping an AI product is easy now. Knowing whether it actually works is still hard. The biggest mistake I see is teams writing evals before they've looked at a single real failure in their product.

Shreya Shankar and I built eight Claude Code skills to fix that. We shaped them by working with over 50 companies and teaching more than 5,000 students in our AI evals course. I walk through all eight, but most of the time goes to the two I'd start with. The first is error discovery, which builds a custom interface for reviewing your traces and keeps sampling new ones until you stop finding new failure modes. The second is the eval audit, which checks your setup against the mistakes we see most often. Get through those two and you'll be ahead of most people working on evals.

title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
description:
A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse.

An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers.

title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
description:
A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work.

Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings.

title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
description:
Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU.

The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself.

title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
description:
An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve.

Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct.

title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
description:
While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop.

Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment.

title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
description:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.

title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
description:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.

title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
description:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.
